title: How Witness Protection Works
summary: Josh and Chuck explain the U.S. Witness Protection Program: its origins in the 1960s Kennedy administration crackdown on organized crime, its creation via the Organized Crime Control Act of 1970 (Sen. John McClellan, aide G. Robert Blakey, and Gerald Shur), the 1984 revision to cover family members, and how witnesses are selected, relocated, given new identities, paid subsistence, and protected during trial. They discuss the program's rules, a 17 percent recidivism figure, a 17-year-old witness who was murdered after returning to Virginia, weaker state and local protection, and programs in other countries. Movie references include Goodfellas (based on Henry Hill) and My Blue Heaven. The episode closes with a listener mail about Clovis people and the Great Plains archaeological record, and a Kiva promo.

segments.title: Opening banter and witnessing crimes
segments.summary: Hosts joke about crimes and discuss the dilemma of witnesses who fear testifying, noting witnesses are sometimes murdered.

segments.title: Origins of the program in the 1960s and 1970 Act
segments.summary: Kennedy administration goes after organized crime in the 1960s. The Organized Crime Control Act of 1970 includes a provision for witness protection, drafted with help from Gerald Shur, and revised in 1984 to cover family members.

segments.title: Goodfellas, My Blue Heaven and Henry Hill
segments.summary: Discussion of popular culture depictions of witness protection, including Goodfellas based on Henry Hill and the trivia that Nicholas Pileggi and Nora Ephron, who married, both based films on interviews with Hill.

segments.title: Eligibility and selection process
segments.summary: Who qualifies: witnesses with major information on organized crime, racketeering, major drug offenses, terrorism, and gangs. Prosecutors apply to the Justice Department's Office of Enforcement Operations, and the Marshals create a dossier including threat assessment. Recidivism rate of about 17 percent is compared with parolees' 40 percent, and over 10,000 convictions are cited.

segments.title: Relocation, new identities and rules
segments.summary: Enrolled witnesses must pay outstanding debts, get new names (often keeping initials), new records with sealed name change, temporary housing, and subsistence payments averaging about $60,000 a year, plus help finding a job. Two key rules: never return to the old area and no contact with past friends and family.

segments.title: Trial security, rule breaking and state programs
segments.summary: Witnesses get round-the-clock protection during transport to trial, with tactics like armored car decoys and the Joseph Barboza case. The Marshals say no follower of the rules has been killed. A 17-year-old gang witness who went back to Virginia was found dead in a river. State and local programs are much weaker.

segments.title: Other countries' programs
segments.summary: Brief mention that Canada, New Zealand, Jamaica, South Africa, Kenya, China and Israel have witness protection programs.

segments.title: Listener mail on Clovis people
segments.summary: Listener Jordan, an archaeologist in Kansas, corrects an earlier episode, noting Clovis sites on the Plains are buried under sediment, creating sampling bias, and that pre-Clovis sites exist across North America.

segments.title: Sign-off and Kiva promo
segments.summary: Hosts promote Kiva team and invite listener email before signing off.
